transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-09-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes | Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Jana (Redwood SE), Laura (CISO - Argent), Malik (Head of Cloud Infra), Priya (Security Engineer), Ethan (Procurement)

[00:00] Avery: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll do a 30 second intro, i'm avery chen on the redwood team, samir and jana from our infra/security folks are here to cover the deep bits on kms and hsm.
[00:10] Laura: thanks, yes we wanted to focus on key management and encryption specifics, making sure nothing lives in a vendor-managed key that we can't control.
[00:18] Malik: also curious about latency/availability impact if we do BYOK w/ external hsm or customer kms.
[00:22] Samir: great, we'll walk through our options. quick overview: redwood supports endpoints with envelope encryption by default; customer data at rest is encrypted and we support multiple KMS integrations (aws kms, gcp kms, azure key vault). we also have options for BYOK where the customer manages the key in their cloud kms and we call it via sts roles and grant.
[00:39] Priya: when you say "we call it" do you mean your service will have access to the plaintext key? that's a hard no for us. we need assurance the key material never leaves our control.
[00:46] Jana: correct, we do envelope encryption so the root key (customer key) is only used to encrypt a per-service data key; redwood never stores the plaintext customer root key. the encrypted data key is what we keep, and it's opaque to us. in cloud kms scenarios, we call the kms api to decrypt the envelope when needed, but the actual key material is always in the customer's kms (we do not import the raw key unless you want a different model).
[01:05] Laura: okay, but we also want an HSM-backed key that we can rotate and that has FIPS 140-2/3 attestation. do you support cloud hsm or on-prem hsm integrations?
[01:13] Samir: yes. we integrate with cloud HSM-backed keys in aws (cloudhsm via aws kms with custom key store), google cloud external key managers, and azure managed hsm. for on-prem the path is a private deployment where the KMS proxy runs in your network and we can call a local HSM via an approved bridge - that requires our private deployment package and a short network design review.
[01:30] Malik: how does key rotation work? can we rotate keys without downtime and how do you handle key revocation/compromise?
[01:36] Jana: rotation is supported via key versioning. the encrypted data keys are stamped with key version metadata; at rotation, new writes use the new data key encrypted under the new root key version. reads still succeed because we keep the previous encrypted data keys and call the corresponding key version in your KMS. revocation is more complex - if you revoke the root key in KMS (disable or schedule deletion), existing data encrypted under past versions will still be decryptable only if the KMS still allows decrypt operations for those versions; if you fully delete your root key, that will render data irrecoverable unless you have backups. we strongly recommend key retirement workflows that keep key versions for a long enough window and a documented incident playbook.
[02:03] Priya: ok that aligns. what about audit logs? we need per-call key usage logs and immutable audit trails for SOC2 and our internal audits.
[02:12] Samir: we can surface a combined audit view. on our side we log the envelope decrypt calls and token-level request IDs; on the KMS side, your KMS logs (cloudtrail / stackdriver / azure monitor) show the KMS decrypt/crypt operations. we recommend correlating the two - we emit structured events with request IDs and timestamps so you can join with your KMS logs. we can also ship syslog/S3/BigQuery of our audit trails if you need centralized retention.
[02:36] Laura: retention is important - we need audit logs stored for 7 years for certain products. can you retain logs or forward them to our archive?
[02:44] Avery: yes, we have options: we can retain telemetry for varying retention tiers (default shorter, enterprise retention as add-on), and we can forward logs to your S3/GCS/Azure blob straight away. that forwarding can be locked down to your storage using least-privilege roles.
[02:58] Malik: slight concern: if every request triggers a KMS call to decrypt a data key, won't that add latency and cost? what's your recommendation?
[03:05] Samir: good question. that's where envelope caching comes in - we cache decrypted data keys in-memory for a TTL that you control, usually a few minutes to balance security and latency. we also do prefix/KV caching for sequences to avoid repeated decrypt cycles per token. for HSM-backed keys, the KMS call overhead is mainly at key unwrap time; after the data key is cached, token generation is local and low latency. we'll provide a matrix of latency impact vs TTL in the POC doc.
[03:34] Priya: caching decrypted keys concerns us from a threat model perspective - if the VM is compromised, an attacker could access cached keys. what mitigations do you have?
[03:43] Jana: we run isolated execution per-tenant and protect the process memory; we also support encrypting the in-memory cache with a transient hardware-bound key where possible (e.g., use of platform TPM or cloud enclave features). for high-security customers, we recommend private deployment with a customer-controlled key-caching proxy inside your VPC so the cache never leaves your environment.
[04:02] Laura: what about SSO and RBAC for key access? we want least privilege so only a small set of service accounts can call decrypt.
[04:09] Samir: we map Redwoods service roles to IAM principals in your KMS via cross-account roles or service accounts. you can restrict permissions to decrypt-only for the specific key. On the Redwood side we enforce RBAC in our control plane so only authorized services can trigger the envelope unwrap path. we can show the IAM policy templates we recommend.
[04:27] Malik: do you support provider-agnostic BYOK like bringing your own key material (imported key) vs referencing keys in our cloud KMS?
[04:33] Jana: both. two common patterns: reference-only where we call your managed key via kms api (recommended), or imported key where you export/import key material into our environment - imported keys are rare because they increase risk; we generally avoid receiving raw key material. If you need to use your own HSM and never expose key material, we recommend a proxy pattern or private deployment.
[04:55] Ethan: procurement question - is HSM support a separate add-on cost and how is it billed?
[05:00] Avery: HSM-backed key support itself is typically part of the enterprise package; cloud provider HSM costs (e.g., AWS CloudHSM or customer KMS usage) are billed by the provider. we can include professional services if you want on-prem setup. we will include pricing in the follow-up.
[05:12] Laura: any regulatory gotchas we should be aware of for EU data residency? we have customers in eu and some data cannot leave the region.
[05:19] Samir: region controls are supported - you can pin workloads to regions, use regional KMS instances, and run private deployments in your region. for hosted mode we ensure data at rest and keys can be region-bound; we can also arrange dedicated capacity in eu regions.
[05:32] Priya: what about emergency key rotation or forced re-encryption? can you rewrap existing encrypted data keys under a new root key en-masse?
[05:40] Jana: yes, we have a rewrap workflow in the platform: we can re-encrypt the data key envelope using a new root key version in a controlled batch job. that process is auditable and can be run during maintenance windows. it does incur compute and potentially downtime for large datasets, but it's designed to be streaming and resumable.
[06:00] Laura: ok good. show me the actual logs we can expect to see - do you have sample cloudtrail entries and redwood event examples?
[06:07] Samir: we do, i'll drop sample snippets in the deck. (shared) Deck link: https://redwood.example.com/security/argent-kms-byo-hsm
[06:15] [00:06:15] Malik: one more technical - how do you handle key access if the KMS region is temporarily unavailable? do you fail closed or fall back to a different key?
[06:23] Jana: by default we fail closed for decrypt calls to prevent silent compromise; however we support configurable fallbacks: you can set a cross-region key replication strategy or allow a pre-authorized fallback key. both have security tradeoffs. we'll recommend a multi-region KMS key with replication for high availability.
[06:40] Priya: are there built-in safeguards to detect unusual key access patterns? we want anomaly detection on decrypt calls.
[06:46] Samir: we emit metrics and alerts for unusual decrypt rates per key; we can integrate with your SIEM - e.g., forward to splunk or sentry. we also have thresholds that can trigger automated rate-limiting or notify the security team.
[06:58] Laura: for SOC2 evidence, will you provide attestation that keys are not accessible by redwood staff?
[07:04] Avery: yes, our SOC2 reports include descriptions of key management processes. for BYOK customers we can provide a tailored attestation and the architecture diagram. for the highest assurance we can do a technical assessment in your environment during private deployment.
[07:18] Ethan: timeline question - if we move forward, how quickly can you stand up a private deployment and run the KMS integration?
[07:24] Jana: typical private deployments range 4-8 weeks including network and HSM provisioning; if you're doing cloud KMS with cross-account roles and not on-prem HSM, we can do a POC in 2-3 weeks.
[07:34] Malik: okay, next steps?
[07:36] Avery: recap: we'll send the BYOK + HSM whitepaper, IAM policy templates, sample audit logs, and a latency/TTL matrix. Priya you'll send your KMS config and any constraints on rotation windows. we'll schedule a follow-up tech deep-dive with your PKI team for the week of 9/20.
[07:50] Laura: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:53] [End of recording]
